metadata.methods_description: Patients with subdural grids and strips were recorded at UCI and CPMC (Nihon Kohden) and at UCSF (Tucker Davis Technologies). Signals not recorded at 1000 Hz were low-pass filtered at 500 Hz and downsampled to 1000 Hz. Patients performed two blocks of 40 instructed-delay reaching trials per arm in counterbalanced order. Kinematics were estimated from button and touch times and are provided at 100 Hz. Neural data are stored as float32 BrainVision files and kinematics as physio TSV files.

The EEG pattern that coincides with this cognitive task is captured, then used to execute an external command, such as operating a neuroprosthetic device. As such, BCIs are dependent on the efficient and reliable interpretation of motor imagery. citation_details.title: Uncovering the Role of the Human Hippocampus in Procedural Motor Learning: Insights from Implicit Sensorimotor Adaptation
citation_details.author: Guillermina Griffa, Agustín Solano, Álvaro Deleglise, Gabriela De Pino, Florencia Jacobacci, Valeria Della‐Maggiore
citation_details.abstract: Recent evidence suggests that the human hippocampus, traditionally associated with declarative memory, plays a role in motor sequence learning (MSL). However, the classic MSL paradigm depends initially on declarative learning. Thus, it is critical to discern whether the participation of the hippocampus relates to its canonical role or to processing a general aspect of learning that transcends the declarative/non-declarative distinction. To address this issue, here we turned to visuomotor adaptation (VMA)-a type of motor learning involving skill recalibration-which unlike MSL can be easily manipulated to eliminate the explicit component. We examined the broader involvement of the hippocampus in procedural motor learning by using diffusion MRI in a sample of males and females to assess structural plasticity associated with memory consolidation in VMA and an implicit-only version (IVMA). We found that both VMA and IVMA engaged the left posterior hippocampus in a learning-specific manner.

citation_details.title: Generalization in motor learning: learning bimanual coordination with one hand
citation_details.author: Yiyu Wang, Madison Weinrich, Yuming Lei, David L. Wright, Milap Singh Sandhu, John J. Buchanan, Deanna M. Kennedy
citation_details.abstract: ABSTRACT The ability to coordinate movements between the hands is crucial for many daily tasks. However, the precise mechanisms governing the storage and utilization of bimanual movement and the distinct contributions of each limb in this process are currently not fully understood. Two key questions persist: 1) How is the neural representation of bimanual coordination stored in the brain, and 2) How is the information governing bimanual coordination shared between hemispheres? In this investigation, we used a virtual partner (VP) to systematically address these issues by allowing the same coordination pattern (CP) to be acquired with unimanual and bimanual movements. More specifically, we used four experimental groups: unimanual (left, right) VP, bimanual, and control conditions. For each condition, retention and transfer tests were administered immediately and 6 hours after the initial practice. The control condition employed the same protocol as unimanual conditions without practice.
